slides.heading: How Brain-Computer Interfaces Work
slides.body: The science turning thought into action — and why it could change everything

slides.heading: What Is a BCI?
slides.body: A brain-computer interface (BCI) is a direct communication pathway between the brain and an external device. It reads electrical signals from neurons and translates them into commands — no muscle movement required.

slides.heading: How the Brain Signals
slides.body: Neurons communicate via tiny electrical spikes called action potentials. BCIs detect these signals using electrodes placed on the scalp, on the brain surface, or implanted directly in brain tissue. More invasive placement = higher signal clarity.

slides.heading: Non-Invasive BCIs
slides.body: EEG headsets sit on the scalp and pick up broad brainwave patterns. They're safe and affordable but noisy. Used in gaming, meditation apps, and early accessibility tools — limited by poor spatial resolution.

slides.heading: Invasive BCIs: Implants
slides.body: Devices like Neuralink's N1 chip embed tiny electrode arrays directly in the cortex. They capture individual neuron firing with far greater precision, enabling paralyzed patients to control cursors or robotic arms with their thoughts alone.

slides.heading: Decoding Intent
slides.body: Raw brain signals are chaotic. Machine learning models train on patterns over hours or days to map specific neural activity to intended actions. The more a user practices, the sharper the signal becomes — the brain adapts too.

slides.heading: Real-World Breakthroughs
slides.body: In 2024–2025, clinical trials saw paralyzed patients type over 90 characters per minute and walk again using neural bypass systems. BrainGate and Synchron's Stentrode reached landmark FDA milestones for wider deployment.

slides.heading: Beyond Medicine: Future Uses
slides.body: Researchers envision BCIs for memory augmentation, seamless AR/VR control, and even brain-to-brain communication. Consumer-grade silent speech interfaces could replace keyboards within a decade.

slides.heading: The Big Ethical Questions
slides.body: Who owns your neural data? Can thoughts be hacked or surveilled? BCI access raises equity concerns — life-changing tech that only wealthy patients or nations can afford risks deepening global divides.

slides.heading: Mind Over Machine
slides.body: BCIs are no longer science fiction — they're in operating rooms and research labs today. The real question isn't whether thought can control technology, but how we ensure that power belongs to everyone.
